metadata.description: Distilled, cross-referenced, and deduplicated chemical engineering heuristics, shortcut design methods, and experience-based rules for conceptual process design, preliminary equipment sizing, and flowsheet synthesis.
metadata.golden_rule: Never use a heuristic rule unless you understand where it came from and how it was derived.

process_synthesis_and_strategy.name: Process Synthesis, Strategy & Flowsheet Hierarchy
process_synthesis_and_strategy.description: Foundational conceptual rules from the Douglas/Turton design hierarchy: Batch vs Continuous, Input/Output structure, Recycle loops, Inerts/Purges, and Energy Pinch.

rules.rule: Never use a heuristic rule unless you understand where it came from and how it was derived.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Heuristics represent condensed empirical wisdom and optimized economic trade-offs (e.g., balancing capital cost vs operating cost at typical utility prices). They are shortcut guides for initial scoping, not physical laws. If process operating conditions deviate from standard commercial ranges (extreme temperatures, pressures, exotic chemistries), heuristics can lead to severe design errors.

quantitative_guidelines.validation_requirement: Apply the PAR Process: Predict using heuristic, Authenticate using rigorous simulation/thermodynamics, Re-evaluate any major discrepancy.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Do not treat heuristics as immutable specifications. Always corroborate with laboratory data, thermodynamic consistency, and safety reviews.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Universally agreed upon as the foundational rule of chemical engineering design across Turton, Walas, and Douglas.

rules.rule: Select continuous processing for annual capacities exceeding 5,000 metric tons/year; select batch processing for capacities below 500 metric tons/year. Evaluate the intermediate range (500-5,000 metric tons/year) based on product flexibility and kinetics.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Continuous processes have higher initial capital investment for automation and piping, but significantly lower labor and operating costs per unit of product at high volume. Batch operations provide equipment versatility for multi-product campaigns, rapid seasonal changeovers, and accommodate slow reaction kinetics (>4-8 hours) or slurry fouling that would plug continuous equipment.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Batch may be mandatory even at high capacities if regulatory validation requires strict lot traceability (e.g. pharmaceuticals, vaccines) or if severe fouling necessitates regular mechanical cleanout.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich quotes 1,000 to 10,000 t/y as the intermediate zone; Turton and Douglas define 500 to 5,000 t/y.

rules.rule: Eliminate inert species upstream of reaction if separation is easily accomplished and catalyst is fouled/poisoned by the inert, but retain the inert if a large exothermic heat of reaction must be moderated.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Inert gases (e.g., N2, CH4) passing through a reactor increase equipment size, downstream compressor duty, and separation loads. However, for highly exothermic reactions, an inert diluent acts as a thermal heat sink, lowering the adiabatic temperature rise and preventing runaway reactions or hot-spots.

quantitative_guidelines.separation_effort: Remove inerts if relative volatility with feed is > 3.0 or condensation is facile.
quantitative_guidelines.exotherm_moderation: Retain inerts if adiabatic temperature rise without inerts exceeds catalyst maximum allowable temperature.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: If downstream separation of inert from products requires cryogenic distillation, upstream removal is strongly favored.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Directly matches Seider Heuristic 3 and Turton Chapter 2 Input/Output heuristics.

rules.rule: Use an excess of an inexpensive, non-toxic, or readily available reactant to drive complete consumption of a valuable, toxic, or hazardous reactant.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Le Chatelier's principle and reaction kinetics dictate that higher concentrations of one reactant accelerate the reaction rate and shift equilibrium toward products. Using excess air, water, or inexpensive hydrocarbon forces near 100% single-pass or overall conversion of the hazardous/costly component, reducing toxic emissions and expensive downstream purification.

quantitative_guidelines.typical_excess: 5% to 50% excess depending on relative raw material costs and equilibrium constants.
quantitative_guidelines.separation_penalty: The excess reactant must be easily separable from the product stream and recycled.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Excess reactant increases recycle flow rate, increasing reactor volume and recycle compressor/pump operating costs. Trade-off optimum must be found.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Consensus rule across Seider (Heuristic 2) and Turton.

rules.rule: Introduce purge streams in recycle loops to provide an exit for trace feed impurities and irreversible side-reaction byproducts. Purge light gases in vapor purges and heavy impurities in liquid purges.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Any material that enters a process and is recycled without an exit mechanism will accumulate indefinitely in the recycle loop until plant operation is disrupted or piping explodes. A purge fraction bleeding 0.5% to 10% of the recycle stream establishes a steady-state impurity concentration.

quantitative_guidelines.vapor_purge: Located at highest point of recycle loop or flash overhead for light boiling components.
quantitative_guidelines.liquid_purge: Located at column bottoms or lowest drainage point for high-boiling polymers/oligomers.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Purge streams inherently carry valuable reactants. If the value of lost reactants exceeds the capital cost of a dedicated separator (e.g. membrane, PSA), install a separation unit instead of a simple purge.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Identical in Seider (Heuristic 4) and Turton (Chapter 2).

rules.rule: Do not purge valuable, toxic, or hazardous species directly to the environment. Install recovery separators to recapture valuable chemicals and reaction/destruction units (scrubbers, flares, incinerators) for hazardous chemicals.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Environmental regulations (EPA, REACH, OSHA) prohibit venting VOCs, toxins, or greenhouse gases. Additionally, raw material yield loss directly destroys process economics.

quantitative_guidelines.destruction_efficiency: Thermal oxidizers / flares typically require >= 98% to 99.9% destruction efficiency.
quantitative_guidelines.scrubbers: Vent scrubbers must achieve outlet concentrations below regulatory Permissible Exposure Limits (PEL).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure flare headers are adequately purged with inert gas to prevent backfire/explosion.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Directly articulated in Seider (Heuristic 5) and Sinnott & Towler (Chapter 1).

rules.rule: Byproducts produced in small quantities by reversible reactions should not be separated for sale or purged; recycle them to extinction in the reactor feed.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: If a byproduct reaction A + B <=> C is reversible, feeding equilibrium concentrations of C back into the reactor prevents net forward reaction of C by Le Chatelier's principle. This increases the overall selectivity of raw materials toward the desired product.

quantitative_guidelines.byproduct_selectivity: Applicable when byproduct formation accounts for < 5-10 mol% of raw material conversion.
quantitative_guidelines.equilibrium_check: Verify that high temperatures do not decompose C into irreversible tars.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Only valid if the byproduct does not poison the catalyst or promote runaway polymerizations.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 6; Turton Section 2.4.2.

rules.rule: For reversible equilibrium-limited reactions, evaluate reactive separation (e.g. reactive distillation) to remove products continuously from the reaction zone, driving conversion far beyond thermodynamic equilibrium.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Conventional systems require large recycle loops and huge separation trains to handle low single-pass conversions. Coupling reaction and distillation in a single column saves capital cost, reboiler energy, and bypasses equilibrium barriers (e.g., methyl acetate synthesis).

quantitative_guidelines.volatility_compatibility: Requires that reaction temperature and distillation temperature ranges overlap significantly, and volatility of at least one product differs from reactants.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Difficult to control if reaction kinetics are very slow relative to vapor-liquid residence times.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 8.

rules.rule: To increase the pressure of a stream, pump a liquid rather than compress a gas, unless refrigeration or reaction phase constraints dictate otherwise.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Mechanical shaft work is proportional to fluid specific volume (dW = V dP). Because liquid density is 100 to 1,000 times higher than gas density, pumping a liquid requires orders of magnitude less electrical power and dramatically smaller capital machinery than gas compression.

quantitative_guidelines.work_ratio: Gas compression work / Liquid pumping work typically ranges from 50:1 to 500:1 for equal mass flow and Delta P.
quantitative_guidelines.condensation_tradeoff: Condensation requires refrigeration or cooling water; if latent heat condensation duty is cheaper than gas compressor power, condense first.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Do not condense if sub-cooling destroys thermal integration or if stream cannot be easily condensed at ambient cooling temperatures.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 43.

rules.rule: Follow the fundamental Pinch Analysis rules: Never transfer heat across the pinch. Above the pinch, only accept heat from hot utilities; below the pinch, only reject heat to cold utilities.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Transferring heat across the pinch creates a double penalty: an equal amount of heat must be added from expensive hot utilities above the pinch AND removed by cold utilities below the pinch. Correct network synthesis minimizes total utility demand.

quantitative_guidelines.delta_T_min_chemical: 10 to 20 K (18 to 36 F) for typical chemical and petrochemical processes.
quantitative_guidelines.delta_T_min_cryogenic: 2 to 5 K (3.6 to 9 F) for cryogenic gas processing where refrigeration power is extreme.
quantitative_guidelines.delta_T_min_furnace: 100 to 200 K for high-temperature flue gases.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Pinch integration couples unit operations; operability, startup flexibility, and safety during unit trips must be preserved.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Chapter 2 (Section 2.6) & Sinnott Chapter 1.

reactors_and_kinetics.name: Reactors & Reaction Kinetics
reactors_and_kinetics.description: Rules for reactor type selection (CSTR vs PFR), heat removal/addition, space velocity, catalyst particle sizing, and reaction-separation coordination.

rules.rule: Select raw materials and chemical reaction pathways to avoid or reduce the handling and storage of hazardous, explosive, and toxic chemicals.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Inherent safety (Kletz principle) is always cheaper and more reliable than add-on protective systems. Substituting less hazardous feedstocks (e.g. producing phosgene in situ in tiny quantities rather than bulk storage) prevents catastrophic community and plant risk.

quantitative_guidelines.inventory_minimization: Minimize intermediate hazardous holdup to < 10-15 minutes of production.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Alternative routes may have lower selectivity or higher raw material costs; perform net present value (NPV) safety-cost tradeoff.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 1; Sinnott & Towler Chapter 1.

rules.rule: Reaction rates must be established experimentally in the laboratory, and residence time or space velocity must eventually be verified in a pilot plant before commercial sizing.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Mass and heat transfer limitations in commercial reactors can severely distort intrinsic chemical kinetics. Pilot plant data validates scale-up models, catalyst longevity, by-product accumulation, and temperature gradients.

quantitative_guidelines.gas_phase_space_velocity: Liquid hourly space velocity (LHSV) typically 0.5 to 5.0 h^-1; Gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) typically 500 to 10,000 h^-1.
quantitative_guidelines.liquid_residence_time: Typically 10 minutes to 4 hours in continuous CSTRs.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Extrapolation of bench-scale microreactor data directly to a large multi-tubular or fluidized bed reactor without CFD or pilot validation causes widespread commercial failures.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.17; Excel sheet 'Reactors'.

rules.rule: For isothermal reactions where reaction rate decreases with conversion (order n > 0), a Plug Flow Reactor (PFR) requires smaller volume than a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor (CSTR). For adiabatic exothermic reactions, a CSTR requires smaller volume at low conversions due to auto-acceleration.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: In a CSTR, the reaction takes place entirely at the lowest reactant concentration (the exit concentration), resulting in the lowest reaction rate throughout. In a PFR, concentration starts high at the inlet, yielding high initial rates and smaller total volume. A series of 3 to 5 CSTRs closely approximates PFR performance.

quantitative_guidelines.cstr_series: N = 3 CSTRs in series achieves 80-90% of PFR volume reduction while retaining agitation and heat transfer capabilities.
quantitative_guidelines.isothermal_pfr_volume: V_PFR / V_CSTR typically 0.1 to 0.5 for high conversions (>85%) with positive order kinetics.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: CSTR is preferred if slurry solids must remain suspended, if reaction generates heavy slurries, or if precise temperature control is critical.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich Appendix C (Reactors, p. 581).

rules.rule: To remove a highly exothermic heat of reaction, use an excess of reactant, an inert diluent, or direct cold-shot fluid injection between adiabatic reaction stages.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: When heats of reaction are extreme (e.g. oxidation, chlorination, hydrogenation), internal cooling tubes or wall jackets lack sufficient surface area per unit volume. Cold shots or diluents directly absorb enthalpy through sensible heat capacity without fouling wall surfaces.

quantitative_guidelines.cold_shot_fraction: Typically 15% to 35% of total feed injected directly into intermediate beds.
quantitative_guidelines.adiabatic_stage_rise: Limit adiabatic temperature rise per bed to 20 to 50 C (36 to 90 F).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Cold shots dilute product stream, increasing downstream separation loads and recycle compressor capacity.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 21; Turton Table 11.17.

rules.rule: For moderately exothermic heats of reaction, circulate reactor fluid to an external heat exchanger, or use a jacketed vessel, internal cooling coils, or intercoolers between adiabatic beds.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: External circulating pump-around exchangers allow very high fluid velocities, high overall heat transfer coefficients (U = 500-1000 W/m2 K), and cleanable heat transfer surfaces unconstrained by vessel shell diameter.

quantitative_guidelines.jacket_area_limit: Jackets are limited to vessel volumes < 15 to 20 m3 (due to surface-to-volume ratio decreasing as 1/D).
quantitative_guidelines.internal_coils: Coils provide up to 2-3x jacket surface area but hinder cleaning and solids suspension.
quantitative_guidelines.pump_around_rate: Pump-around flow is typically 5 to 20 times the fresh feed flow rate.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure circulating pumps can handle reactor operating temperatures, pressures, and any entrained particulate matter.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 22; Turton Table 11.17.

rules.rule: For highly endothermic reactions, use excess preheated reactant, an inert carrier (e.g. steam), or hot shots. For moderately endothermic reactions, circulate through an external heater, use jackets, or install interheaters between stages.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Endothermic reactions (e.g. catalytic reforming, ethylbenzene dehydrogenation) cause steep temperature drops that extinguish reaction kinetics. Superheated steam or fired interheaters maintain the reaction in the active kinetic regime.

quantitative_guidelines.inert_carrier_ratio: Steam-to-hydrocarbon molar ratios of 5:1 to 15:1 are common in dehydrogenations.
quantitative_guidelines.interheater_duty: Reheats stream back to inlet temperature (typically 500 to 650 C).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Steam carrier requires extensive condensation and wastewater treatment downstream.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 23 and 24.

rules.rule: Select catalyst particle sizes based on reactor contact regime: ~0.10 mm (100 microns) for fluidized beds; ~1 mm for slurry bubble columns; 2 to 5 mm (1/8 to 3/16 inch) pellets or extrudates for fixed packed beds.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: In fixed beds, smaller particles increase internal pore diffusion efficiency (effectiveness factor) but cause excessive pressure drops (Ergun equation: Delta P scales as 1/d_p^2). Pellets of 2-5 mm represent the optimum trade-off between pressure drop and intraparticle diffusion. In fluidized beds, Geldart Group A/B powders (~0.1 mm) fluidize smoothly without slugging.

quantitative_guidelines.pressure_drop_fixed_bed: Limit gas Delta P to < 0.1 to 0.3 bar per meter of catalyst bed.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Particles smaller than 1 mm in fixed beds lead to severe bed plugging and dust carryover.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Consensus values in Turton Table 11.17, Seider, and Excel sheet 'Reactors'.

rules.rule: Fluidized beds maintain nearly uniform temperature (within 5 C throughout) and exhibit well-stirred behavior when L/D < 2; they approach plug flow when L/D > 4. In packed bed reactors, bed height must be at least half the diameter (H >= 0.5D) to ensure uniform flow distribution.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Intense solid circulation in bubbling fluid beds provides massive effective thermal conductivity. When L/D is low, backmixing dominates; tall narrow beds (L/D > 4) limit axial mixing. In packed beds, very shallow beds suffer from maldistribution and wall bypass channeling.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Fluid bed solids must be robust against attrition; cyclones required to recapture fines.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich & Vasudevan Appendix C (Reactors, p. 581).

rules.rule: For homogeneous stirred tank reactors, specify agitator power input of 0.5 to 1.5 hp/1000 gal (0.1 to 0.3 kW/m3). If heat transfer coils/jackets are installed, increase to 1.5 to 3.0 hp/1000 gal (0.3 to 0.6 kW/m3). For gas dispersion or severe slurry suspension, specify up to 5 to 10 hp/1000 gal (1.0 to 2.0 kW/m3).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Mechanical agitation enhances boundary layer heat transfer coefficients at vessel walls/coils and ensures homogeneous temperature, preventing localized hot-spots that degrade product quality.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Agitator mechanical dissipation converts directly into heat; in cryogenic or heat-sensitive bioreactions, motor heat can overwhelm refrigeration.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.17; Excel sheet 'Reactors'.

separations_distillation_and_absorption.name: Separations: Distillation & Gas Absorption
separations_distillation_and_absorption.description: Comprehensive design rules for tray columns, packed towers, column sequencing, reflux ratios, HETP correlations, pressure selection, and internals sizing.

rules.rule: Distillation is the primary, most economical method for separating miscible liquid mixtures when relative volatility alpha > 1.10. If alpha < 1.05, components form an azeotrope, or mixtures are heat-sensitive, use liquid-liquid extraction, extractive/azeotropic distillation, or crystallization.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Distillation utilizes vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) driven by direct heat addition, avoiding external mass-separating agents that must themselves be recovered. However, as alpha approaches 1.0, required reflux ratios and tray counts approach infinity, causing capital and reboiler energy costs to explode.

quantitative_guidelines.difficult_distillation: 1.05 <= alpha <= 1.10 (requires high tray count or extractive agent)
quantitative_guidelines.uneconomical_distillation: alpha < 1.05 (switch to extraction, crystallization, or membranes)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Does not apply if operating temperature exceeds thermal degradation/polymerization threshold of the chemicals.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 9; Ulrich Appendix C (Separators, p. 579).

rules.rule: For multi-component distillation trains, apply the standard sequencing heuristics: 1. Perform the easiest separation first (highest relative volatility). 2. Remove corrosive, hazardous, or polymerizable species early. 3. Remove the most plentiful component (highest molar flow) first. 4. Reserve difficult separations (lowest alpha) until last. 5. Reserve high-purity product specifications until last. 6. Favor sequences yielding equimolar splits between distillate and bottoms.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Removing plentiful or easy components first reduces the total mass flow sent to downstream columns, dramatically shrinking column diameters and reboiler duties. Doing the hardest separation in the presence of non-key components wastes energy boiling non-participating species.

quantitative_guidelines.direct_sequence: Lightest component taken overhead column-by-column (favored when feed is mostly light components).
quantitative_guidelines.indirect_sequence: Heaviest component taken bottoms column-by-column (favored when feed is mostly heavy components).
quantitative_guidelines.equimolar_split: Molar ratio D / B between 0.8 and 1.2 minimizes column thermodynamic irreversibility.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Heuristics may conflict with one another (e.g. most plentiful component has the lowest alpha). In such cases, use shortcut marginal vapor rate calculations or simulator case studies to break ties.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Identical guidelines across Turton (Table 11.13), Seider, Ulrich (p. 579), and Excel sheet 'Tray Towers'.

rules.rule: Operate distillation columns at the lowest feasible pressure, because relative volatility increases as pressure decreases. The minimum operating pressure is constrained by the cooling medium in the condenser (condenser temperature >= 40-49 C for cooling water); the maximum operating pressure is constrained by bottom reboiler degradation temperature or column critical pressure.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Vapor pressure ratios and VLE non-idealities widen at lower pressures, reducing the required theoretical stages and reflux. However, cooling tower water cannot cool condensers below ~40 C (104 F) without expensive refrigeration. At the column base, bottoms temperature must not cause thermal decomposition, coking, or exceed the critical point of the mixture.

quantitative_guidelines.cooling_water_condenser_temp: >= 40 C (104 F) minimum, typically 45 to 50 C (113 to 122 F)
quantitative_guidelines.vacuum_threshold: Use vacuum if bottoms temperature at 1 atm exceeds thermal degradation limit

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Vacuum distillation requires larger column diameters due to high vapor specific volumes, and increases air inleakage risk.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.13; Ulrich p. 579; Excel sheet 'Tray Towers'.

rules.rule: Set the operating reflux ratio R between 1.1 and 1.5 times the minimum reflux ratio (R_min), with 1.2 to 1.3 R_min being the standard economic optimum. Set the operating number of theoretical stages N between 1.5 and 2.0 times the minimum stages (N_min).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Total annualized cost equals capital cost (trays/shell) plus operating cost (reboiler steam and condenser cooling). At R = R_min, infinite stages are required (infinite capital). At high R, reboiler and condenser sizes and energy consumption explode. The total cost curve has a flat optimum between 1.15 and 1.30 R_min.

quantitative_guidelines.underwood_equations: Used to compute R_min from feed thermal condition q and relative volatilities.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: When pinch occurs near the feed tray or in highly non-ideal / azeotropic mixtures, Gilliland correlations deviate; use rigorous stage-by-stage simulation.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider recommends 1.1-1.2 R_min; Turton recommends 1.2-1.5 R_min; Ulrich recommends 1.2-1.3 R_min.

rules.rule: Use tray columns for column diameters > 0.6 to 0.9 m (2 to 3 ft), high liquid flow rates, fouling fluids, slurries, or when internal cooling coils/side draws are needed. Use packed columns for vacuum distillation (where pressure drop is critical), highly corrosive systems (ceramic/plastic packings), foaming liquids, and small diameters (< 0.6 m).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Trays are structurally robust, easy to clean, and maintain predictable liquid holdup. However, packed columns provide significantly lower pressure drop per theoretical stage (0.1 in H2O/ft vs 2-4 in H2O per tray), making packing mandatory for deep vacuum distillation to prevent excessive bottom reboiler temperatures.

quantitative_guidelines.diameter_boundary: Trays favored for D > 0.9 m (3 ft); Packings favored for D < 0.6 m (2 ft)
quantitative_guidelines.pressure_drop_comparison: Tray Delta P ~ 1 kPa/stage (~0.15 psi/stage); Packed Delta P ~ 0.1 to 0.3 kPa/stage
quantitative_guidelines.vacuum_advantage: Packed columns reduce reboiler temperature by 10-30 C in vacuum services compared to trays.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Packed towers with D > 1.5 m require precision liquid distributors every 3 to 6 m of bed height to prevent liquid wall channeling.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Consensus across Turton (Tables 11.14 & 11.15), Ulrich (p. 580), and Excel sheets 'Tray Towers' & 'Packed Towers'.

rules.rule: Standard tray spacing is 18 to 24 inches (0.45 to 0.60 m); use 12 inches (0.3 m) for small, clean columns; use 24 to 36 inches (0.6 to 0.9 m) for foaming liquids, high vapor velocities, or to provide manways for internal inspection. Tray efficiency typically ranges from 60% to 85% for low-viscosity hydrocarbons (< 0.5 cP), dropping below 30% for viscous liquids (> 2 cP) and gas absorbers.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Tray spacing must provide sufficient disengagement height for entrained liquid droplets to separate from rising vapor before reaching the tray above. Viscous liquids retard liquid-phase molecular diffusion, drastically reducing mass transfer rates and tray Murphree efficiency.

quantitative_guidelines.standard_tray_spacing: 24 inches (0.6 m) is standard industrial default.
quantitative_guidelines.small_column_spacing: 18 inches (0.45 m) or 12 inches (0.3 m) for D < 1.2 m.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Weeping occurs at low vapor rates (< 40-50% design); entrainment flooding occurs at high vapor rates (> 80-85% flooding velocity).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.14; Excel sheet 'Tray Towers'.

rules.rule: Calculate tray tower active height using the verified Ulrich equation: H_a = (N * H_t) / epsilon_t, where stage height H_t = 0.5 * D^0.3 for D > 1.0 m, and H_t = 0.5 m for D <= 1.0 m. Total tower height equals active height plus 1.0 to 1.5 m for vapor disengagement at the top and 2.0 to 3.0 m for bottom liquid holdup.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: As column diameter increases, liquid cross-flow path and vapor throw increase, requiring larger tray spacing (modeled empirically by H_t = 0.5 D^0.3) to prevent premature jet flooding.

quantitative_guidelines.max_shell_height: Maximum practical single shell height is 50 to 60 m (160 to 200 ft); split into two shells if stages exceed this limit.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure L/D ratio of total column does not exceed 20 to 25 to prevent wind-load structural vibration without guy wires.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich p. 580; Verified against visual scan.

rules.rule: Calculate packed tower active height using the verified Ulrich equation: H_a = N * HETP. For distillation, HETP = 0.5 * D^0.3 (for D > 0.5 m); for gas absorption, HETP = D^0.3; for both distillation and absorption when D <= 0.5 m, HETP = D. Limit individual packed bed heights to 6 m (20 ft) before installing liquid redistributors.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Height Equivalent to a Theoretical Plate (HETP) increases with column diameter because liquid distribution is never perfectly uniform, leading to radial concentration gradients. In gas absorption, higher liquid film resistance increases HETP compared to distillation.

quantitative_guidelines.packing_sizing_rule: Use 1-inch (25 mm) packing for gas flow < 500 cfm (14 m3/min); use 2-inch (50 mm) packing for gas flow > 2000 cfm (57 m3/min).
quantitative_guidelines.diameter_ratio: Column diameter / packing diameter >= 10 to 15 to prevent wall bypass.
quantitative_guidelines.max_bed_height: 4 to 6 m (15 to 20 ft) per packed segment.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: High-efficiency structured packings can achieve HETP of 0.2 to 0.4 m regardless of diameter, provided precision multi-point distributors (>= 100 drip points/m2) are installed.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich p. 580; Turton Table 11.15; Excel sheet 'Packed Towers'.

rules.rule: In physical and chemical gas absorption columns, the exit gas temperature is typically within 2 C of the entering liquid absorbent temperature.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Because the heat capacity flow rate of the entering liquid absorbent is typically significantly larger than that of the gas stream, the exiting gas reaches thermal equilibrium with the cold entering liquid at the top of the tower.

quantitative_guidelines.heat_of_absorption: Exothermic heat of absorption creates a temperature bulge in the middle or bottom of the column; intercoolers may be required if solvent loading capacity drops significantly with temperature.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: In cases with low liquid-to-gas ratios (L/G < 1.0) and high gas temperatures, gas may exit hotter than liquid feed.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich Appendix C (Gas Absorption, p. 579).

separations_liquid_liquid_extraction.name: Separations: Liquid-Liquid Extraction (LLE)
separations_liquid_liquid_extraction.description: Rules for solvent selection, phase dispersion, contactor equipment (mixer-settlers, agitated columns, centrifugal extractors), and theoretical stage requirements.

rules.rule: Specify liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) when components have low relative volatility (alpha < 1.05), form close-boiling azeotropes, contain non-volatile or inorganic solutes, or involve thermally sensitive materials (biochemicals, polymers) where distillation temperatures cause degradation.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Extraction operates at ambient or near-ambient temperatures, avoiding thermal decomposition. However, extraction introduces a foreign solvent that must be recovered downstream (usually by distillation), making extraction a two-unit separation system that must be economically justified against direct distillation.

quantitative_guidelines.volatility_boundary: alpha < 1.05 or boiling point difference Delta T_b < 5 C
quantitative_guidelines.temperature_advantage: Can operate at 20 to 50 C, avoiding 150+ C distillation conditions.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure solvent can be completely stripped from the raffinate and extract streams without creating secondary azeotropes.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.16; Seider Rule 9; Ulrich p. 579.

rules.rule: Select extraction solvents satisfying: 1. High selectivity (beta = (y_A/x_A) / (y_B/x_B) >= 5 to 10). 2. High distribution coefficient (K_D >= 1.5 to 2.0). 3. Density difference Delta rho >= 0.05 to 0.10 g/cm3 (50 to 100 kg/m3) for rapid gravity phase disengagement. 4. Interfacial tension gamma = 5 to 25 mN/m (dyne/cm). 5. Chemical stability, non-toxicity, and easy downstream solvent recovery.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: High selectivity minimizes required theoretical stages. High distribution coefficient minimizes required solvent-to-feed ratio (S/F), reducing solvent circulation pump and distillation stripper sizes. A density difference < 0.05 g/cm3 causes slow settling and severe phase entrainment. Interfacial tension < 1 mN/m promotes stable emulsions that resist coalescence.

quantitative_guidelines.density_difference: Delta rho >= 0.05 to 0.10 g/cm3 (50 to 100 kg/m3)
quantitative_guidelines.interfacial_tension: 5 to 25 mN/m (values < 1-2 mN/m form unseparable emulsions; values > 40 mN/m require excessive agitation power)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Solvents with high flammability, toxicity, or environmental persistence (PFAS) should be avoided in modern inherently safe design.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.16; Walas Chapter 16.

rules.rule: Most commercial extraction cascades require 4 to 10 theoretical stages. Select equipment based on stage requirements: 1. Mixer-settlers for 1 to 4 stages, large volumetric capacities, and when high stage efficiency (80-90% per mixer) is required. 2. Agitated columns (Karr, Scheibel, Kühni, RDC) for 4 to 12 stages, moderate floor space, and systems with low interfacial tension. 3. Centrifugal extractors (Podbielniak) for rapid contact (< 10 s residence time), hazardous/radioactive systems, or dense emulsions.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Unagitated packed/sieve extraction columns suffer from very poor stage efficiency (10-20% per theoretical stage) due to droplet coalescence. Mechanical agitation provides controlled droplet breakup, maintaining high interfacial area per unit volume.

quantitative_guidelines.theoretical_stages: Typically 4 to 8 stages (rarely > 12 to 15 stages in a single column).
quantitative_guidelines.settler_superficial_velocity: 0.5 to 1.5 gpm/ft2 (1.2 to 3.6 m3/(h m2)) for gravity settling.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Mixer-settlers consume extensive plot footprint; column contractors consume vertical space but minimize ground area.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.16; Ulrich Appendix C.

rules.rule: Disperse the phase with the higher volumetric flow rate in column extractors to maximize interfacial mass transfer area, unless that phase has significantly higher viscosity. Alternatively, disperse the phase that does not preferentially wet the column internals.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Dispersing the larger volumetric flow creates a higher holdup fraction of droplets, increasing interfacial area (a = 6 * phi / d_32). However, if the dispersed phase preferentially wets the metal/plastic internals, droplets coalesce into large sheets, destroying interfacial area.

quantitative_guidelines.dispersed_phase_holdup: Operating droplet holdup fraction phi is typically 10% to 25% (flooding occurs above 30-35%).
quantitative_guidelines.wetting_rule: The continuous phase should preferentially wet the internals (contact angle < 90 deg).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: If mass transfer resistance resides predominantly in the continuous phase, dispersing the other phase may be optimal.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Walas Chapter 16; Turton Table 11.16.

separations_solids_and_slurries.name: Separations & Processing: Solids and Slurries
separations_solids_and_slurries.description: Rules for crystallization (cooling, evaporative, melt), multiple-effect evaporators, filtration, centrifugation, solids drying, particle size reduction/enlargement, and solids conveying.

rules.rule: Crystallize inorganic chemicals from concentrated aqueous solutions by cooling/chilling when solubility decreases sharply with temperature; use evaporative crystallization when solubility is nearly temperature-independent (e.g. NaCl). Separate organic compounds by melt crystallization (suspension or layer crystallization) when close-boiling isomers or solid eutectics are present.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Cooling crystallization requires only sensible heat removal and is energy-efficient when dC*/dT is steep. For flat solubility curves, cooling produces negligible yield, requiring water evaporation to induce supersaturation. Melt crystallization operates near freezing points without solvents, achieving ultra-high purities (> 99.9%) for isomers (e.g. p-xylene).

quantitative_guidelines.chilling_crystallization: Maintain solution at most 1 to 2 F (0.5 to 1 C) below saturation temperature.
quantitative_guidelines.evaporative_crystallization: Common for flat solubility curves or when solvent evaporation and crystallization occur simultaneously in vacuum crystallizers.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Organic melts that form solid solutions rather than simple eutectics require multi-stage fractional crystallization or zone refining.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 12 and 14; Excel sheet 'Crystallization'.

rules.rule: Control crystallizer growth rate and crystal size distribution by limiting the supersaturation ratio S = C / C_sat tightly in the range 1.02 to 1.05. Growth rates are roughly equal in all crystallographic directions, but crystals are never perfect spheres.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Operating within the metastable zone (S = 1.02 - 1.05) allows solute to deposit onto existing seed crystals without triggering uncontrolled homogeneous secondary nucleation, preventing a flood of unfilterable sub-micron fines.

quantitative_guidelines.temperature_depression: Delta T_subcooling = 1 to 2 F (0.5 to 1.1 C) below saturation.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Trace impurities or tailored habit modifiers can dramatically accelerate or poison growth along specific crystal faces.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Identical in Seider Heuristic 13 and Excel sheet 'Crystallization'.

rules.rule: In multiple-effect evaporators, recover and reuse latent heat across stages. Steam economy scales approximately as: 1 effect ~ 0.8 kg vapor/kg steam; 2 effects ~ 1.6; 3 effects ~ 2.4; N effects ~ 0.8N. Optimum number of effects is 4 to 6 when boiling point elevation (BPE) > 4 C (7 F); up to 8 to 10 effects when BPE is negligible.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Vapor boiled off in one effect is condensed at lower pressure in the heating tubes of the next effect. However, dissolved compounds cause boiling point elevation (BPE), which consumes available temperature driving force across the train. High BPE reduces the net Delta T available, limiting the practical number of effects.

quantitative_guidelines.steam_economy_formula: Economy ~ 0.8 * N  (kg evaporated / kg live steam)
quantitative_guidelines.small_bpe_effects: 8 to 10 effects (when BPE is near zero)
quantitative_guidelines.heat_transfer_threshold: If overall U < 500 W/(m2 K) in any effect, switch evaporator type or rearrange feed sequence.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Steam-jet thermocompressors or mechanical vapor recompression (MVR) should be evaluated to boost low-pressure vapors when electricity is cheaper than boiler fuel.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 15; Ulrich Appendix C (Evaporators, p. 576); Excel sheet 'Evaporation'.

rules.rule: In multiple-effect evaporator trains, select flow arrangement based on feed temperature and viscosity: 1. Use forward feed (liquid and vapor flow co-currently from high to low pressure) for hot liquid feeds and fewer stages, as liquid flows by pressure differential without intermediate pumps. 2. Use backward/reverse feed (liquid pumped counter-currently from low to high pressure) for cold feeds and solutions that become highly viscous as they concentrate.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: In backward feed, the most concentrated, viscous syrup is heated by the hottest prime steam in the first effect, maximizing heat transfer coefficients (U) and minimizing required heat transfer area, though intermediate transfer pumps are required.

quantitative_guidelines.forward_feed_criteria: Use forward feed if U_1 > U_last by less than 50% and feed is near boiling point.
quantitative_guidelines.forced_circulation_velocity: 15 to 20 ft/s (4.5 to 6.0 m/s) in tube passes to suppress boiling inside tubes and prevent scaling.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Backward feed requires reliable canned or magnetic drive pumps capable of handling boiling slurry feeds under vacuum.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 16; Ulrich p. 576; Excel sheet 'Evaporation'.

rules.rule: Size vaporizers and evaporators using the verified Ulrich equation for superficial vapor velocity: u = 0.06 * sqrt((rho_l - rho_g) / rho_g). If calculated diameter exceeds 4 m, specify a horizontal vessel, multiple vertical vessels, or specialized entrainment separators. Allow one additional diameter for vapor disengagement; if total height > 4 * diameter, install internal heating coils.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Superficial vapor velocity is limited by droplet entrainment (modified Souders-Brown form with k = 0.06 m/s). Exceeding this velocity causes liquid carryover into vapor piping and downstream condensers.

quantitative_guidelines.max_height_to_diameter: H_total <= 4 * D_vessel (use internal coils if exceeded).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure demister pads are installed if mist carryover poisons downstream catalysts.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich & Vasudevan Appendix C (Evaporators and Vaporizers, p. 575); verified against high-resolution visual scan.

rules.rule: Classify slurry filtration rates using a laboratory vacuum leaf test: 1. Rapid filtering (cake buildup 0.1 to 10 cm/s): use top-feed horizontal belt filters, pan filters, or pusher centrifuges. 2. Medium filtering (buildup 0.1 to 10 cm/min): use rotary vacuum drum or disk filters. 3. Slow filtering (buildup 0.1 to 10 cm/h): use plate-and-frame filter presses, leaf pressure filters, or sedimenting centrifuges.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Fast-filtering slurries settle rapidly and require top-feed designs to avoid plugging feed troughs. Slow-filtering slurries have high specific cake resistance, requiring high driving pressures (3 to 15 bar in a filter press) that vacuum filters (limited to ~0.8 bar Delta P) cannot provide.

quantitative_guidelines.continuous_filter_limit: Do not specify continuous filtration if at least 0.35 to 0.5 cm cake cannot form in under 5 minutes.
quantitative_guidelines.filter_sludge_solids: Dewatered filter sludges typically contain ~50 wt% solids.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Rotary drum precoat filters (using diatomaceous earth) are required for dilute, slimy, or gelatinous solids that blind standard filter media.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 17; Ulrich p. 582; Excel sheet 'Filtration'.

rules.rule: Specify solid-bowl / decanter centrifuges for continuous liquid-solid clarification when cake solids may contain fines and mother liquor purity is flexible. Specify basket / peeler / centrifugal filters when thorough cake washing and minimum residual moisture content are required.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Solid-bowl decanters rely on centrifugal sedimentation (G-forces 1,000 to 4,000 g) without a filter media, preventing blinding from slimy solids. Perforated basket centrifuges filter through a cloth, achieving thorough displacement washing and low cake moisture.

quantitative_guidelines.settling_velocity_limit: Use centrifuges when gravity settling velocity is < 0.001 m/s.
quantitative_guidelines.slurry_concentration: Helical conveyor centrifuges suitable for high-solids slurries (10 to 50 wt% solids).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Centrifuges have high rotating kinetic energy; avoid handling pyrophoric or explosive mixtures without nitrogen inerting.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 18; Ulrich p. 581.

rules.rule: Select solids drying equipment based on particle size and physical state: 1. Granular solids (3 to 15 mm): continuous tray or belt dryers (drying time 10-200 min). 2. Small free-flowing particles (1 to 3 mm): pneumatic flash conveying dryers (air velocity 10-30 m/s, residence time ~1 min). 3. Very small particles (< 1 mm): fluidized bed dryers. 4. Free-flowing heat-tolerant bulk solids: rotary cylindrical dryers (residence time 5-90 min, air velocity 1.5-3.0 m/s). 5. Pastes and viscous slurries: drum dryers (contact time 3-12 s). 6. Solutions and pumpable slurries: spray dryers (drying time a few seconds).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Spray and flash dryers expose enormous interfacial surface area per unit volume, evaporating moisture in seconds to prevent heat damage. Rotary dryers tumble robust minerals in a heavy shell with flights for gentle convective drying.

quantitative_guidelines.rotary_dryer_time: 5 to 90 minutes; drum rpm * D(ft) = 15 to 25; 85% free cross-sectional area.
quantitative_guidelines.drum_dryer_time: 3 to 12 seconds; flakes 1 to 3 mm thick; max evap ~3,000 lb/h (1,360 kg/h).
quantitative_guidelines.pneumatic_dryer_air_velocity: 33 to 100 ft/s (10 to 30 m/s); residence time ~1 minute.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure exhaust air dust collectors (baghouses or cyclones) are grounded to prevent electrostatic dust explosions.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 19 & 20; Excel sheet 'Drying Solids'.

rules.rule: Select solids conveying equipment based on material properties: 1. Small, low-density, non-sticky, non-abrasive particles (< 3 mm): pneumatic conveying with air at 1 to 7 ft3 air/ft3 solids (0.03 to 0.5 m3/m3) and velocity 35 to 120 ft/s (11 to 37 m/s) for distances up to 400 ft (120 m). 2. Sticky, abrasive, or lumpy solids: screw conveyors or bucket elevators for distances up to 150 ft (45 m). 3. Bulk, non-sticky solids of any size: belt conveyors for long distances (up to miles), with inclinations up to 30 degrees.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Pneumatic conveying encloses dust within piping, ideal for plant transfer without spills. Abrasive materials erode pipe elbows, requiring mechanical transport (belts/screws). Belt conveyors handle huge tonnage with minimum specific energy consumption.

quantitative_guidelines.pneumatic_velocity: 35 to 120 ft/s (11 to 37 m/s); pressure 6 to 12 psig (0.4 to 0.8 bar)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Do not use pneumatic conveying for explosive dusts without inert N2 conveying gas or explosion suppression vents.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 48; Ulrich p. 574; Excel sheet 'Conveyors'.

rules.rule: Apply size reduction in stages: 1. Coarse crushing: Jaw crushers (reduce lumps 4 in-3 ft to 1-4 in); Gyratory crushers (slabby feed 8 in-6 ft to 1-10 in); Cone crushers (secondary reduction of 2 in-1 ft to 0.2-2 in). 2. Fine grinding: Rod mills (reduce feed up to 20 mm to 10-35 mesh); Ball mills (reduce 1-10 mm to < 140 mesh / < 100 microns); Fluid energy / jet mills (reduce to ultrafine 0.1 to 1.0 micron).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Comminution energy follows Rittinger/Bond laws (energy scales with new surface area generated). Single-stage reduction from meter-scale rocks to micron powder causes extreme mechanical jamming and energy inefficiency.

quantitative_guidelines.jaw_crusher_feed: 0.1 to 1.0 m (4 in to 3 ft) -> product 25 to 100 mm (1 to 4 in)
quantitative_guidelines.gyratory_crusher_feed: 0.2 to 2.0 m (8 in to 6 ft) -> product 25 to 250 mm

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Wet milling requires 20-30% less power than dry milling but introduces downstream slurry filtration steps.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 49 & 50; Ulrich p. 574–575.

rules.rule: For particle size enlargement: 1. Use rotary compression tableting presses for extreme uniformity in size and weight (pharmaceuticals/catalysts up to 1.5 in). 2. Use roll compactors and pellet mills for high-capacity briquetting. 3. Use screw extruders for pastes and melts. 4. Use rotating drum or disk granulators with liquid binders for bulk fertilizers (2 to 25 mm). 5. Use prilling towers for melt droplets solidified into uniform spheres.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Fine powders create dust hazards, poor flowability in hoppers, and cake during shipping. Agglomeration, tableting, and prilling convert powders into free-flowing, dust-free bulk granules.

quantitative_guidelines.prilling_requirement: Material must possess sharp melting point and low melt viscosity.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Prilling towers require substantial vertical height (30 to 60 m) to ensure complete droplet freezing before hitting the tower floor.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 51; Ulrich p. 582.

rules.rule: Separate solids by size: 1. Grizzly bars for particles > 5 cm (2 in). 2. Revolving screens (trommels) for 6 to 38 mm (0.25 to 1.5 in). 3. Flat vibrating screens for 3 to 80 mesh (0.18 to 6 mm). 4. Air classifiers for fine powders < 80 mesh (< 180 microns). 5. Cyclones to remove solid particles or liquid droplets down to 10 microns from gas streams. 6. Hydroclones to remove solid particles down to 5 microns from liquids.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Screens below 80 mesh blind rapidly due to electrostatic forces and moisture capillary bridging; air classifiers use centrifugal and drag forces to separate sub-sieve particles cleanly. Cyclones use centrifugal acceleration (50 to 500 g) to throw particles against walls without moving parts.

quantitative_guidelines.cyclone_gas_cutoff: >= 10 microns (d_50 ~ 5-10 um; Delta P ~ 5 to 15 kPa / 2 to 6 in H2O)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Cyclones cannot collect sub-micron dust; baghouses or electrostatic precipitators are required for particles < 1-2 microns.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 52 & 53; Ulrich p. 581–582.

heat_transfer_exchangers_and_furnaces.name: Heat Transfer: Exchangers, Furnaces & Boilers
heat_transfer_exchangers_and_furnaces.description: Rules for shell-and-tube heat exchangers, tube dimensions, fluid allocation, LMTD F-factor, U-values, minimum approach Delta T, reboiler nucleate boiling limits, and fired furnaces.

rules.rule: For standard shell-and-tube heat exchangers, specify 3/4-inch (19.05 mm) OD tubes on a 1-inch (25.4 mm) triangular pitch, with standard tube lengths of 16 ft (4.88 m) or 20 ft (6.10 m). A 1-ft (30 cm) diameter shell contains approximately 100 ft2 (9.3 m2) of surface area; area scales roughly with D_shell^2.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: The 3/4-inch tube on 1-inch triangular pitch provides the optimal balance between high surface area density, turbulent flow friction, and external tube cleaning access. Triangular pitch provides 15% more heat transfer area than square pitch for the same shell diameter (use square pitch only if shell-side mechanical cleaning is required).

quantitative_guidelines.tube_pitch: 1.0 inch triangular (1.25 * OD) for clean fluids; 1.0 inch square for mechanical cleaning
quantitative_guidelines.shell_area_rule_of_thumb: Shell diameter 1 ft -> ~100 ft2; 2 ft -> ~450 ft2; 3 ft -> ~1,100 ft2 (Area ~ 100 * D(ft)^2.15)
quantitative_guidelines.max_shell_diameter: Typically 1.2 to 1.5 m (48 to 60 inches); split into parallel shells if larger.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: For viscous fluids with shell-side Reynolds number < 2000, 1-inch tubes on square or rotated square pitch reduce pressure drop.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Identical in Turton Table 11.11, Seider, and Excel sheet 'Heat Exchangers'.

rules.rule: Allocate fluids between tube side and shell side according to the standard priority hierarchy: 1. Tube side: corrosive fluids (alloys needed only for tubes/channels, not thick shell), fouling/scaling streams (easier mechanical cleaning), high-pressure streams (> 10 bar, avoids thick shell wall), high-temperature streams, and toxic fluids. 2. Shell side: viscous liquids (baffles promote turbulence and cross-flow), condensing vapors, boiling liquids, and streams requiring low pressure drop.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Building high-pressure or corrosion-resistant metallurgy into the shell wall is prohibitively expensive compared to containing it within thin-walled tubes. Shell-side baffles induce cross-flow turbulence at much lower Reynolds numbers (Re ~ 200) than straight tube interiors (Re ~ 2300), benefiting viscous fluids.

quantitative_guidelines.pressure_threshold: Put fluid > 10-15 bar on tube side.
quantitative_guidelines.fouling_velocity: Maintain tube-side liquid velocity at 1.5 to 2.5 m/s (5 to 8 ft/s) for cooling water to prevent silt deposition.
quantitative_guidelines.plate_exchanger_limit: Plate-and-frame exchangers are not recommended for pressures exceeding 10 bara.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: If both fluids are corrosive and high-pressure, double-pipe or special all-alloy welded blocks are required.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.11; Ulrich p. 577–578; Excel sheet 'Heat Exchangers'.

rules.rule: Calculate required heat exchanger surface area from: A = Q_dot / (U * F * LMTD). Maintain the LMTD correction factor F >= 0.80 to 0.90 (use F = 0.90 as initial shortcut). If calculated F < 0.80, a severe temperature cross exists; switch to multiple shells in series or a true countercurrent 1-1 exchanger.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: In multi-pass shell-and-tube exchangers (e.g. 1-2 TEMA E), shell-side fluid flows both co-currently and counter-currently relative to tube passes. When F drops below 0.80, the LMTD correction curve plunges steeply, making the exchanger unstable and hypersensitive to minor flow or temperature fluctuations.

quantitative_guidelines.heat_loss_allowance: Allow up to 5% to 10% heat loss depending on shell operating temperature.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Do not use simple LMTD if fluid heat capacity (Cp) varies significantly with temperature or during non-linear condensation of multi-component mixtures; perform zone-by-zone enthalpy analysis.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.11; Ulrich p. 578; Excel sheet 'Heat Exchangers'.

rules.rule: Specify near-optimal minimum approach temperatures (Delta T_min) based on temperature regime: 1. Sub-ambient / cryogenic temperatures: <= 10 F (5.5 C) or down to 2-3 C for refrigeration circuits. 2. Ambient up to 300 F (150 C): 20 F (11 C) for liquids and high-U systems. 3. High temperatures and gases: 50 F (28 C) for low-U systems. 4. Fired furnaces: 250 to 350 F (140 to 195 C) between flue gas exit and inlet process fluid.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Approach Delta T represents the economic trade-off between heat exchanger capital cost (which approaches infinity as Delta T -> 0) and operating utility cost. In cryogenic service, refrigeration work is extremely expensive (Carnot efficiency: W = Q*(T_ambient - T_cold)/T_cold), justifying huge exchanger area to achieve tight approach.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: In heat integration networks, reducing Delta T_min below 10-15 C can cause uncontrollable heat oscillations between coupled distillation towers.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 26; Ulrich p. 578; Turton Table 11.11.

rules.rule: Use standard typical overall heat transfer coefficients (U) for preliminary scoping: 1. Liquid-to-liquid (water/organics): 300 to 900 W/(m2 K) [50 to 160 Btu/(hr ft2 F)]. 2. Gas-to-gas: 15 to 50 W/(m2 K) [3 to 10 Btu/(hr ft2 F)]. 3. Boiling water / steam reboiler: 1,500 to 4,000 W/(m2 K) [260 to 700 Btu/(hr ft2 F)]. 4. Condensing steam to liquid: 1,000 to 2,500 W/(m2 K) [175 to 440 Btu/(hr ft2 F)]. 5. Condensing hydrocarbons: 300 to 800 W/(m2 K) [50 to 140 Btu/(hr ft2 F)].
rules.explanation_and_derivation: The overall resistance (1/U) is the sum of internal film, external film, metal wall, and two fouling resistances. Because gas heat transfer coefficients are very low (~20-80 W/m2 K), gas-gas exchangers require extended surfaces (fins) or enormous areas. Phase-change boiling and condensation achieve very high film coefficients (> 3,000 W/m2 K).

quantitative_guidelines.organic_organic: 200 to 500 W/(m2 K) [35 to 90 Btu/(hr ft2 F)]
quantitative_guidelines.gas_gas: 15 to 50 W/(m2 K) [3 to 10 Btu/(hr ft2 F)]
quantitative_guidelines.air_cooled_exchanger_liquid: 300 to 700 W/(m2 K) [50 to 120 Btu/(hr ft2 bare tube F)]
quantitative_guidelines.air_cooled_exchanger_gas: 50 to 200 W/(m2 K) [10 to 35 Btu/(hr ft2 bare tube F)]

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Always account for fouling resistances: add R_f = 0.0002 to 0.0004 (m2 K)/W for process hydrocarbons, and 0.0002 (m2 K)/W for treated cooling water.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.11; Ulrich Table 4.15 & p. 578; Excel sheet 'Heat Exchangers'.

rules.rule: Estimate typical allowable pressure drops in heat exchangers: 1. Liquid heating, cooling, or boiling: 0.2 to 0.6 bar (3 to 9 psi, standard 5 psi / 0.35 bar). 2. High-viscosity liquids: 0.5 to 0.7 bar (7 to 10 psi). 3. Condensing vapors or gas streams: 0.05 to 0.15 bar (0.7 to 2.0 psi, standard 0.1 bar / 1.5 psi). 4. Process fluids passing through fired furnaces: 1.4 bar (20 psi).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Pumping power and piping head loss dictate reasonable economic pressure drops. Gas streams have low absolute pressures and large volumetric rates, making high pressure drops unacceptable due to compressor operating costs.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: In deep vacuum condensers, allowable Delta P is strictly limited to < 0.01 to 0.03 bar (< 5 to 15 mmHg) to protect column top pressure.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 31; Ulrich p. 578; Turton Table 11.11.

rules.rule: In reboilers and vaporizers, maintain the maximum overall temperature driving force Delta T_driving <= 45 F (25 C) to ensure nucleate boiling and avoid film boiling burnout.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: When the temperature difference between tube wall and boiling liquid exceeds the critical Delta T (~25 C / 45 F), boiling transitions from nucleate to film boiling. A continuous vapor film blankets the tube surface, acting as a thermal insulator that collapses the boiling heat transfer coefficient by 80% to 90%.

quantitative_guidelines.critical_heat_flux: Limit heat flux q/A to < 35,000 to 50,000 W/m2 (11,000 to 16,000 Btu/(hr ft2)) for boiling organics.
quantitative_guidelines.thermosiphon_submergence: Maintain liquid level in column sump so that 100% of reboiler tube length is submerged.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: High-boiling heavy hydrocarbons with severe fouling tendencies require lower Delta T (< 15-20 C) to prevent tube wall skin coking.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 28; Turton Table 11.11.

rules.rule: Specify fired heaters/furnaces when process fluid temperatures must exceed 750 F (400 C). Hydrocarbon combustion yields an adiabatic flame temperature of ~3,500 F (1,925 C); supply 15% to 25% excess air to ensure complete combustion and limit firebox flue gas to 2,000 F (1,100 C). Set stack gas temperature at 650 to 950 F (340 to 510 C) or > 300 F (150 C) with an economizer/air preheater to prevent acid dew-point condensation.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Steam headers cannot practically supply heat above ~250-300 C, and synthetic heat transfer oils degrade above 350-400 C. Fired heaters burn fuel gas/oil directly. Flue gases contain SO2/SO3; if stack temperature drops below the sulfurous/sulfuric acid dew point (~130-150 C), catastrophic acid corrosion destroys ducts and stacks.

quantitative_guidelines.temperature_cutoff: Use fired furnace if T_process > 400 C (750 F)
quantitative_guidelines.excess_air: 10% to 20% for natural gas; 15% to 25% for fuel oil
quantitative_guidelines.max_firebox_temp: 2,000 F (1,100 C) to protect tube support metallurgy
quantitative_guidelines.thermal_efficiency: 75% to 80% without air preheat; 85% to 92% with air preheat/economizer.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Do not exceed maximum film temperature for thermally degradable feeds (e.g. vacuum residue, ethylene cracking).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 25 & 30; Ulrich p. 576; Turton Table 11.11.

rules.rule: Quench very hot process streams (> 1,150 F / 620 C, e.g. reactor effluents) to below 1,150 F before sending to shell-and-tube exchangers for additional cooling/condensation. Use recycled downstream cold liquid, cold reactant, or liquid water as the direct-contact quench fluid.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Above 600-650 C, heavy hydrocarbons rapidly crack into carbonaceous coke on metallic heat exchanger surfaces, destroying heat transfer and causing tube pluggage. Direct liquid quench evaporates instantly, cooling the gas in milliseconds.

quantitative_guidelines.quench_fluids: Downstream recycled liquid, cold feed, or boiler feedwater.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Quenching with water adds steam to the process stream, which must be condensed and handled in downstream wastewater systems.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 32.

rules.rule: Specify double-pipe or multi-pipe hairpin heat exchangers when required heat transfer area is small (< 100 to 200 ft2 / 10 to 20 m2), or when operating pressures are very high (> 100 bar).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Shell-and-tube exchangers have significant fixed fabrication costs for tube sheets, shell flanges, and channel covers that are uneconomical for small duties. Double-pipe units consist of standard pipe fittings, provide true pure countercurrent flow (F = 1.0), and easily withstand extreme pressures.

quantitative_guidelines.pipe_sizes: Typically 2-inch pipe inside 3-inch pipe, or 3-inch inside 4-inch.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Uneconomical for large heat loads (> 50 m2) due to excessive footprint, manifold piping, and leak points.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.11 (Rule 9); Excel sheet 'Heat Exchangers'.

cooling_towers_and_refrigeration.name: Cooling Towers, Utilities & Refrigeration
cooling_towers_and_refrigeration.description: Rules for cooling water temperatures, cooling tower approach, utility steam distribution headers, refrigeration tonnage, and refrigerant selection.

rules.rule: Standard cooling tower water is supplied to process exchangers at 85 to 90 F (29 to 32 C) and returned at a maximum allowable temperature of 115 to 120 F (46 to 49 C). In European/temperate climates, design for 30 C supply and 45 C return.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Above 120 F (49 C), calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate solubility drops sharply (inverse solubility), causing severe mineral scale formation on heat exchanger tube walls. This scaling drastically degrades heat transfer (scaling resistance R_f surges) and restricts flow passages.

quantitative_guidelines.supply_pressure: Typically 3 to 5 barg (45 to 75 psig) at battery limit.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: In arid or cold climates, cooling water can be supplied at 20 to 25 C, allowing tighter condenser temperatures.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 27 (90 F in, 120 F max out); Ulrich p. 573 (30 C in, 45 C out); Turton Table 11.18.

rules.rule: Industrial mechanical-draft cooling towers cool circulating water to within 5 to 10 F (3 to 5.5 C) of the ambient air wet-bulb temperature, typically achieving 90% of theoretical saturation.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Evaporative cooling is limited by the ambient wet-bulb temperature. Closing the approach below 5 F requires exponentially larger tower packing volume and fan horsepower.

quantitative_guidelines.cooling_range: 15 to 25 F (8 to 14 C) Delta T across the tower
quantitative_guidelines.drift_loss: < 0.005% of circulating water rate with modern drift eliminators
quantitative_guidelines.evaporation_loss: ~1% of circulating flow rate per 10 F (5.6 C) of cooling range
quantitative_guidelines.blowdown_cycles: Cycles of concentration typically maintained between 3 and 7.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Wet-bulb temperatures vary seasonally; base design on summer 1% or 2% ASHRAE/meteorological wet-bulb design values.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.18; Excel sheet 'Cooling Towers'.

rules.rule: Specify utility steam distribution at standardized header pressure levels: 1. High Pressure (HP): 40 to 45 bara (580 to 650 psig), 400 C (750 F) superheated. 2. Medium-High Pressure: 33 bara (480 psig), 239 C sat. 3. Moderate / Medium Pressure (MP): 10 to 17 bara (150 to 250 psig), 185 to 205 C sat. 4. Medium-Low Pressure: 9 bara (130 psig), 175 C sat. 5. Low Pressure (LP): 3.5 to 5.0 bara (50 to 75 psig), 140 to 155 C sat.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Standardizing header pressures enables cogeneration (expanding HP steam through backpressure turbines to generate electricity while exhausting MP/LP steam for process reboilers).
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Steam lines must be sloped with steam traps every 30 to 50 m to remove condensate and prevent water hammer.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich p. 573; Turton Table 11.18; Excel sheet 'Refrigeration & Utilities'.

rules.rule: One ton of refrigeration equals the heat removal rate of 12,000 Btu/h = 12,660 kJ/h = 3.517 kW. Estimate compressor work per ton: ~1.0 hp/ton (0.75 kW/ton) at 40 F (4 C) evaporator temperature; ~2.0 hp/ton (1.5 kW/ton) at 0 F (-18 C); ~3.5 hp/ton (2.6 kW/ton) at -40 F (-40 C); and up to 5 to 7 hp/ton at -100 F (-73 C).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Carnot cycle thermodynamics govern coefficient of performance (COP = T_cold / (T_hot - T_cold)). As refrigeration temperature drops, compressor pressure ratio and power per kilowatt of cooling surge exponentially.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: For evaporator temperatures below -30 C, use two-stage compression with economizer flash intercooling; below -60 C, use two-fluid cascade systems (e.g. ethylene-propylene).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.18; Excel sheet 'Refrigeration & Utilities'.

rules.rule: Select refrigerants according to required process temperature level: 1. Above 0 C (32 to 50 F): chilled water. 2. 0 to -15 C (14 to 32 F): chilled aqueous glycol or calcium chloride brine. 3. -10 to -45 C (-50 to 14 F): Ammonia (NH3), Propane (R-290), or R-134a. 4. -45 to -100 C (-150 to -50 F): Ethylene, Ethane, or two-fluid cascade cycles. 5. Below -100 C: Cryogenic expander / nitrogen Claude cycles.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Refrigerants must maintain positive suction pressure (> 1 bara / 14.7 psia) at the evaporator to prevent atmospheric air and moisture inleakage, and reasonable condenser discharge pressures (< 15 to 20 bar) to allow condensation using cooling tower water.

quantitative_guidelines.ammonia_range: -33 C to +35 C (atmospheric boiling point = -33.3 C / -28 F)
quantitative_guidelines.propane_range: -42 C to +40 C (atmospheric boiling point = -42.1 C / -44 F)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ammonia is toxic and flammable (B2L); propane/ethylene are highly flammable (A3); ensure safety zoning in accordance with API RP 500 / EN 378.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.18; Ulrich p. 574; Excel sheet 'Refrigeration & Utilities'.

fluid_handling_pumps_and_piping.name: Fluid Handling: Pumps & Piping Hydraulics
fluid_handling_pumps_and_piping.description: Rules for pump selection (centrifugal, reciprocating, gear), pump power formulas, NPSH cavitation margins, liquid/gas piping sizing, and control valve allowances.

rules.rule: Select pump type based on flow rate, differential head, and fluid viscosity: 1. Centrifugal pumps: primary choice for heads up to 3,200 ft (1,000 m) and flow rates of 10 to 5,000 gpm (2 to 1,200 m3/h) with low to moderate viscosities (< 200 cP). 2. Reciprocating positive displacement pumps: for ultra-high heads up to 20,000 ft (6,000 m) and moderate/low flows (< 500 gpm / 115 m3/h), or precise chemical dosing. 3. Rotary gear/screw pumps: for viscous liquids (> 200 to 100,000 cP) at heads up to 3,000 ft and flows < 1,500 gpm. 4. Axial flow pumps: for high volumetric flow rates (20 to 100,000 gpm) at very low differential head (< 40 ft / 12 m).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Centrifugal pumps impart kinetic energy via impeller rotation; their efficiency drops precipitously above 100-200 cP due to disk friction. Positive displacement pumps trap discrete fluid packets, making flow independent of discharge pressure and highly efficient for thick viscous fluids.

quantitative_guidelines.centrifugal_max_head: Single-stage up to 600 ft (180 m); multi-stage up to 3,200 ft (1,000 m)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Centrifugal pumps require minimum continuous flow (spillback line) to prevent overheating and internal recirculation damage.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 37; Turton Table 11.9; Ulrich p. 580; Excel sheet 'Pumps'.

rules.rule: Calculate pumping hydraulic power from: Theoretical Horsepower THp = (gpm * Delta P (psi)) / 1714, or in metric units: Shaft Power P (kW) = [1.67 * Flow (m3/min) * Delta P (bar)] / eta. Centrifugal pump efficiencies typically range from 45% at 10-20 gpm up to 80-85% at 1,000+ gpm.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Hydraulic power is the dot product of volumetric flow and total dynamic pressure rise (W_dot = Q * Delta P). Pump shaft power includes mechanical seal, bearing, and hydraulic recirculation losses.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: For liquids with specific gravity != 1.0, verify motor sizing using actual liquid density: BHP = THp * SG / eta.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 39; Turton Table 11.9; Excel sheet 'Pumps'.

rules.rule: Ensure Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHA) exceeds Net Positive Suction Head Required (NPSHR) by at least 2 to 3 ft (0.6 to 1.0 m) safety margin: NPSHA >= NPSHR + 0.6-1.0 m. For boiling liquids at bubble point in column sumps or reflux drums, NPSHA is generated solely by the static elevation head of the liquid above the pump centerline minus suction pipe friction.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: If pressure at the impeller eye falls below the liquid vapor pressure, vapor bubbles form and violently collapse against the impeller metal (cavitation), creating extreme acoustic shock waves that pit the metal and destroy bearings/seals within hours.

quantitative_guidelines.suction_elevation_boiling: Elevate distillation column skirt by 2.5 to 4.5 m (8 to 15 ft) to provide required 2 to 4 m NPSHA for bottoms pump.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Hydrocarbons with dissolved light ends have higher vapor pressures than pure components; verify true bubble point pressure.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.9; Excel sheet 'Pumps'.

rules.rule: Size liquid process piping based on standard economic velocity and pressure drop guidelines: 1. Pump discharge lines: size for velocity v = (5 + D/3) ft/s [~1.5 to 2.5 m/s] and pressure drop Delta P ~ 2.0 psi/100 ft of pipe (0.45 bar/100 m). 2. Pump suction lines: size for velocity v = (1.3 + D/6) ft/s [~0.5 to 1.2 m/s] and pressure drop Delta P ~ 0.4 psi/100 ft of pipe (0.09 bar/100 m), where D is pipe inner diameter in inches. Ulrich guideline: 1 to 4 m/s for general liquids.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Pipe diameter reflects the classic economic balance between pipe capital cost (which increases with D) and pumping electrical power (which scales inversely with D^5 by the Darcy-Weisbach equation). Suction lines are sized larger with lower velocity to prevent suction cavitation.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: For abrasive slurries, limit velocity to < 1.5-2.0 m/s to prevent pipe erosion; for settling slurries, maintain velocity above minimum deposition velocity (~1.2-1.5 m/s).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.8; Ulrich p. 573; Excel sheet 'Piping'.

rules.rule: Size gas, vapor, and steam piping for velocity v = 20 * D ft/s (where D is nominal diameter in inches) or typically 15 to 30 m/s (50 to 100 ft/s), with allowable pressure drop Delta P ~ 0.5 psi/100 ft of pipe (0.1 bar/100 m). For low-pressure gases (< 2 bar), size for 3 to 10 m/s; for vacuum vapor lines, limit pressure drop to < 0.1 psi/100 ft.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Due to low gas density, high velocities are economical without excessive pressure drop. However, velocities exceeding 30-40 m/s generate excessive aerodynamic noise, acoustic vibration, and erosion at pipe elbows.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: In corrosive or wet-gas service, limit velocity to < 15-20 m/s to prevent stripping of protective oxide/corrosion inhibitor films (API RP 14E erosional velocity: v_e = C / sqrt(rho)).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.8; Ulrich p. 573; Excel sheet 'Piping'.

rules.rule: In hydraulic circuits, allocate at least 10 psi (0.7 bar) or 25% to 33% of total dynamic system friction across control valves to ensure stable flow controllability. For each 10-ft (3.05 m) rise in liquid elevation, allocate 4.0 to 4.3 psi (0.28 to 0.30 bar) static head pressure drop for water-like liquids (Delta P_static = rho * g * Delta z).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: A control valve must represent a significant fraction of total circuit resistance to modulate flow effectively. If line friction dominates (> 90%), closing the valve has little effect until it is nearly seated, causing severe control hunting and non-linearity.

quantitative_guidelines.static_elevation_head: 4.0 psi per 10 ft of elevation (for water / SG=1.0)
quantitative_guidelines.metric_static_head: 0.1 bar per meter of elevation (for water)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure control valve sizing factor C_v operates between 20% and 80% open during normal turndown to avoid seat cavitation.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 38; Turton Table 11.8.

gas_compression_and_vacuum.name: Gas Compression, Vacuum & Power Recovery
gas_compression_and_vacuum.description: Rules for fans, blowers, compressors, multi-stage compression with intercooling, air inleakage formulas, steam-jet ejectors, liquid-ring vacuum pumps, and turboexpanders.

rules.rule: Select gas moving equipment based on required differential pressure: 1. Fans: for Delta P < 40 in H2O gauge (1.47 psig / 10.1 kPa / 0.1 bar) near atmospheric pressure; gas density variation < 10%; efficiencies 60-80%. 2. Blowers: for Delta P from 3 kPa to 30 psig (0.03 to 2.0 barg / 5 bar absolute); efficiencies 70-85%. 3. Compressors: for high-pressure operation from 2 barg up to 3,000 bar; efficiencies 60-80%.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Fans operate in the nearly incompressible fluid regime where blades move large gas volumes against low duct resistance. Blowers compress gas moderately. Compressors handle significant density changes and extreme mechanical stresses, requiring cooling and heavy casings.

quantitative_guidelines.blower_pressure_range: 3 kPa to 2.0 barg (30 psig / up to 5 bara)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Gas compression generates significant heat; discharge temperatures must not exceed 150-200 C to protect seals, lube oils, and prevent gas auto-ignition.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 34; Ulrich p. 576–577; Turton Table 11.10; Excel sheet 'Compressors and Vacuum'.

rules.rule: Limit the compression ratio per stage to r_p = P_out / P_in <= 3.5 to 4.0. For overall pressure ratios > 4.0, stage the compressors with intercooling between stages. Staging guideline: P_final / P_inlet < 4 -> 1 stage; 4 to 16 -> 2 stages; 16 to 64 -> 3 stages; 64 to 256 -> 4 stages. Allocate approximately equal compression ratios across all stages, and assume 2 psi (15 kPa / 0.15 bar) pressure drop through each intercooler.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: High compression ratios cause excessive discharge temperatures (T_out = T_in * (P_out/P_in)^((k-1)/k)), which breakdown lubricating oils and cause mechanical seizure. Staging with intercoolers approaches isothermal compression, reducing total electrical power by 15% to 30% and knocking out condensed liquids.

quantitative_guidelines.intercooler_cool_temp: Cool gas back down to 35 to 45 C (95 to 115 F) with cooling water.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure knock-out drums are installed downstream of every intercooler to remove condensed liquid droplets before the next compression stage.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 36; Ulrich p. 577; Turton Table 11.10; Excel sheet 'Compressors and Vacuum'.

rules.rule: Calculate theoretical adiabatic horsepower THp and exit temperature T_2 for gas compression from: THp = SCFM * [T_1 / (8130 * a)] * [(P_2 / P_1)^a - 1], and exit temperature: T_2 = T_1 * (P_2 / P_1)^a, where a = (k - 1) / k, with k = C_p / C_v, T in deg R, and SCFM at 60 F and 1 atm (379 SCF/lbmol). Shaft brake horsepower BHP = THp / eta_ad.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Derived from isentropic expansion thermodynamics for an ideal gas. Polytropic or adiabatic efficiency accounts for internal fluid shear, turbulence, and blade losses.

quantitative_guidelines.typical_k_values: k ~ 1.4 for air/diatomics (a = 0.286); k ~ 1.25 to 1.30 for methane/hydrocarbons (a = 0.20 to 0.23).
quantitative_guidelines.adiabatic_efficiency: eta_ad = 0.65 to 0.78 for centrifugal; 0.75 to 0.85 for reciprocating.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: At high pressures (> 50 bar), real gas compressibility (Z) must be included: multiply power by Z_avg = (Z_1 + Z_2)/2.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 35; Turton Table 11.10; Excel sheet 'Compressors and Vacuum'.

rules.rule: Estimate ambient air inleakage into vacuum equipment from: w = k * V^0.667, where w is air inleakage in lb/hr, V is total equipment internal volume in ft3, and k is the pressure-dependent leakage factor: k = 0.20 for P > 90 torr; k = 0.15 for 21 to 89 torr; k = 0.10 for 3.1 to 20 torr; k = 0.051 for 1 to 3 torr.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Air leaks through flanged joints, sight glasses, valve packings, and pump shaft seals. Because leak locations occur at perimeter seals rather than internal volume, inleakage scales with equipment surface area (V^(2/3)). At deeper vacuum, higher differential pressure drives higher critical sonic flow through microscopic crevices.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Add 20% to 50% safety factor for agitator stuffing boxes, rotary sight glasses, or equipment with numerous flanged nozzle connections.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 44; Turton Table 11.10; Walas.

rules.rule: If the temperature of gas sent to a vacuum system exceeds 100 F (38 C), install a pre-condenser using cooling water upstream of the vacuum unit. The gas leaving the condenser will be saturated at a dew point of 100 F at prevailing vacuum pressure.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Volumetric flow rate under vacuum is massive. Condensing condensable organic or water vapors before the ejector/vacuum pump reduces volumetric loading by 80% to 95%, dramatically shrinking ejector size and motive steam consumption.

quantitative_guidelines.temperature_cutoff: Install pre-condenser if T_gas > 100 F (38 C)
quantitative_guidelines.condenser_exit_dew_point: 100 F (38 C) at prevailing vacuum pressure.
