rules.conditions_and_limitations: In deep vacuum (< 10-20 torr), water vapor will not condense at 38 C; chilled water or surface desublimation is required.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristic 45; Turton Table 11.10.

rules.rule: Specify vacuum producing machinery according to pressure and flow: 1. Liquid-ring vacuum pumps: for pressures down to 10 torr (13 mbar) and volumetric capacities up to 10,000 cfm (17,000 m3/h). 2. Steam-jet ejectors: for pressures down to 2 torr (2.7 mbar) and massive gas capacities up to 1,000,000 cfm (1,700,000 m3/h). Staging: 1 stage for 100 to 760 torr; 2 stages for 15 to 100 torr; 3 stages for 2 to 15 torr. A 3-stage steam ejector reaching 2 torr requires ~100 lb of 100 psig steam per lb of gas.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Steam ejectors have zero moving parts, tolerate corrosive and dusty vapors, and have very low capital cost. However, thermodynamic efficiency is low (25-30%), requiring significant motive steam. Liquid-ring pumps have higher mechanical efficiency but require seal fluid cooling.

quantitative_guidelines.steam_consumption_3_stage: ~100 lb steam (100 psig) per lb non-condensable gas at 2 torr

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Direct-contact barometric condensers between ejector stages generate large volumes of contaminated wastewater; surface condensers are preferred for hazardous organics.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 46 & 47; Ulrich p. 577; Turton Table 11.10.

rules.rule: Evaluate power recovery expanders / turboexpanders when more than 20 to 100 kW (25 to 130 hp) of shaft power can be recovered from a high-pressure gas stream. Evaluate hydraulic pressure-recovery turbines for liquids when recoverable power exceeds 100 to 150 hp (75 to 110 kW). For lower recoveries, use throttling valves.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Expanding high-pressure gas across a turbine produces isentropic work and deep cryogenic cooling. Expanding high-pressure liquid (e.g. rich amine from a high-pressure absorber) across a reverse-running pump/hydraulic turbine recovers 50% to 75% of pumping power.

quantitative_guidelines.turboexpander_max_temp: Radial flow turboexpanders limited to inlet T <= 550 C [Ulrich p. 575].

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Gas expansion across a turbine causes condensation (wet expansion); limit liquid condensation at turbine exhaust to < 10-15 wt% to avoid blade erosion.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Seider Heuristics 40, 41, 42; Ulrich p. 575; Turton Table 11.5; Excel sheet 'Drivers'.

pressure_vessels_and_storage.name: Pressure Vessels, Drums & Storage
pressure_vessels_and_storage.description: Rules for vessel orientation, L/D ratios, liquid holdup times, Souders-Brown gas-liquid separator sizing, liquid-liquid decanters, design pressure/temperature margins, and storage tanks.

rules.rule: Specify liquid surge drums as horizontal vessels; specify gas-liquid vapor separators, knockouts, and flash drums as vertical vessels. The optimum length-to-diameter ratio L/D is typically 3.0, with an allowable economic range of 2.5 to 5.0. Process drums commonly range up to 4 m (13 ft) in diameter and 20 m (65 ft) in length.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Horizontal orientation provides a large liquid surface area and shallow liquid depth, ideal for decanting immiscible phases and liquid surge. Vertical orientation minimizes vessel footprint and provides maximum disengagement height between vapor inlet nozzle and mist eliminator pad to prevent re-entrainment.

quantitative_guidelines.max_standard_diameter: 4.0 m (13 ft) due to highway/rail transport limits; larger vessels require field welding
quantitative_guidelines.wall_thickness: t = (P * R) / (S * E - 0.6 * P) + C_corrosion (ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code Sec VIII).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: For very large gas-liquid separation flows, horizontal knockouts with wire mesh pads may be required if vertical diameter exceeds 4.5 m.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.6; Ulrich p. 579; Excel sheet 'Drum Vessels'.

rules.rule: Size liquid surge drums based on standard holdup/residence times: 1. Reflux drums (half-full): 5 minutes holdup based on overhead distillate plus reflux flow. 2. Drums feeding another distillation column: 5 to 10 minutes holdup to absorb upstream upsets. 3. Drums feeding a fired furnace/boiler: 30 minutes holdup to prevent dry-tube firing during unit trips. 4. Compressor suction knock-out drums: sized for 10 times the maximum expected liquid accumulation per minute. 5. Flash drums: 5 to 10 minutes (300 to 600 s) liquid residence time.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Liquid holdup cushions downstream equipment against upstream control upsets, valve stiction, and feed fluctuations. A fired furnace requires generous holdup because losing liquid feed while burners are firing causes catastrophic tube rupture within minutes.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: In batch or campaign transfers, design feed drums for 8 hours capacity (one shift) or 1,800 s minimum.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.6; Ulrich p. 580; Excel sheet 'Drum Vessels'.

rules.rule: Calculate maximum allowable vapor velocity in gas-liquid separators using the Souders-Brown equation: v_vapor = k * sqrt((rho_l - rho_v) / rho_v). Values of k: k = 0.35 ft/s (0.107 m/s) with a horizontal mesh de-entrainment pad; k = 0.167 ft/s (0.051 m/s) with a vertical mesh pad; k = 0.10 ft/s (0.030 m/s) without a mesh pad. Standard mesh pad thickness is 6 inches (150 mm), with 6 to 18 inches disengagement before the pad and 12 inches after.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: The Souders-Brown formula balances upward drag force on entrained liquid droplets against downward gravitational settling force. The k-factor accounts for droplet coalescence in knitted wire mesh pads.

quantitative_guidelines.disengagement_space: 6 to 18 inches before pad, 12 inches after pad to gas outlet.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: At high operating pressures (> 40-50 bar), vapor density approaches liquid density and surface tension collapses; reduce k by 20% to 40% (GPSA guidelines).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.6; Excel sheet 'Drum Vessels'; Seider Heuristic 53.

rules.rule: Size horizontal liquid-liquid decanters / phase separators for gravity settling velocities of 2 to 3 inches/min (0.85 to 1.27 mm/s). Typical residence times are 300 to 600 s (5 to 10 min), with vessel L/D ratios of 2.0 to 4.0.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Decantation relies on Stokes' law settling of dispersed droplets through a continuous immiscible phase. Because droplets are small (~100-200 microns) and density differences may be modest, horizontal plug flow with minimal turbulence is required.

quantitative_guidelines.overflow_weir: Install adjustable overflow weir or siphon loop to maintain interfacial level.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: If settling velocity is < 0.001 m/s (< 2.4 in/min), gravity settling drums are impractical; install coalescer mesh/vane packs, centrifugal separators, or chemical demulsifiers.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.6; Ulrich p. 580; Excel sheet 'Drum Vessels'.

rules.rule: Set pressure vessel design pressure at 10% or 10 to 25 psi (0.69 to 1.7 bar) above maximum operating pressure, whichever is greater (maximum operating pressure is typically at least 25 psi / 1.7 bar above normal operating). Set design temperature 25 C (50 F) above maximum operating temperature for operation between -30 and 345 C (-22 to 653 F).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Design margins prevent relief valves from simmering or lifting during normal operational swings. ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII) requires formal design pressure/temperature envelopes for mechanical stress rating.

quantitative_guidelines.design_pressure_margin: Max(10% above max operating, 10 to 25 psi / 0.7 to 1.7 bar)
quantitative_guidelines.design_temperature_margin: +25 C (+50 F / 77 F in Excel) above max operating temperature
quantitative_guidelines.minimum_design_pressure: Standard atmospheric vessels rated for at least 50 psig (3.5 barg) if steam cleanout is possible
quantitative_guidelines.full_vacuum_rating: Vessels operating under vacuum or susceptible to steam condensation must be designed for full external vacuum (15 psi external / 1.0 bar external).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Above 345 C (653 F), allowable metal stress drops rapidly due to metal creep; design temperature margins increase to 50 C.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.7; Sinnott & Towler Chapter 1; Excel sheet 'Pressure and Storage Vessels'.

rules.rule: Specify 30 days of storage capacity for raw materials and finished products to ensure uninterrupted plant operation against supply chain or transport delays. Ensure bulk storage tanks are sized at least 1.5 times the size of the delivery transport vessel (tanker truck, railcar, barge). Day tanks are designed with ~8 hours capacity (one operating shift).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Storage decouples continuous chemical processing from discrete shipping logistics. Sizing at >= 1.5x delivery vessel volume guarantees that a transport carrier can be unloaded immediately even if the tank is not completely empty.

quantitative_guidelines.internal_transfer_residence: 1,800 s (30 min) for feed tanks; allow 15 min per batch transfer shift [Ulrich p. 583]
quantitative_guidelines.atmospheric_storage_types: Cone roof for non-volatile liquids; floating roof or internal blanket for volatile VOCs (P_vap > 1.5 psia / 0.1 bar).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Pressurized gases (LPG, propylene) stored in pressurized bullets or spheres (Horton spheres) designed to API 620/650 standards.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich p. 583; Turton Table 11.7; Excel sheet 'Pressure and Storage Vessels'.

mixing_and_agitation.name: Mixing & Agitation
mixing_and_agitation.description: Rules for agitation intensity, volumetric power consumption (kW/m3, hp/1000 gal), impeller types and tip speeds, tank geometry, baffles, and gas spargers.

rules.rule: Specify agitation power based on process mixing intensity: 1. Mild blending of miscible liquids: 0.2 to 0.5 hp/1,000 gal (0.03 to 0.10 kW/m3). 2. Moderate reaction and heat transfer: 0.5 to 1.5 hp/1,000 gal (0.10 to 0.30 kW/m3) [Ulrich quotes 0.3 to 0.7 kW/m3 for miscible liquids]. 3. Intense agitation / solids suspension: 1.5 to 3.0 hp/1,000 gal (0.30 to 0.60 kW/m3). 4. Gas dispersion / heavy slurries: 4.0 to 10.0 hp/1,000 gal (0.80 to 2.0 kW/m3).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Power per unit volume (P/V) determines turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate (epsilon), which governs micro-mixing, droplet breakup in liquid-liquid systems, and boundary layer heat transfer at vessel walls.

quantitative_guidelines.superficial_fluid_velocities: Mild agitation: 0.10 to 0.20 ft/s (0.03 to 0.06 m/s); Intense: 0.70 to 1.0 ft/s (0.21 to 0.30 m/s).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: In non-Newtonian or highly viscous fluids (> 50-100 Pa s), turbine impellers only mix a cavern near the hub; use helical ribbon or anchor agitators.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.17; Ulrich p. 578; Excel sheet 'Mixing'.

rules.rule: Select impeller types based on service: 1. Marine propellers: high speed (400 to 1750 rpm), axial flow, low shear; diameters seldom exceed 0.5 m. 2. Flat-blade turbines (Rushton turbines): high shear, radial flow, for gas dispersion and droplet breakup; diameters typically 0.3 to 0.5 times vessel diameter (D_impeller / D_vessel = 0.3 to 0.5), limited to ~3 m. 3. Hydrofoil impellers: high pumping efficiency for solids suspension at low power.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Axial flow impellers maximize bulk circulation (pumping number N_q), making them energy-efficient for blending and solid suspension. Radial flat-blade turbines maximize turbulent shear (power number N_p = 5.0), required to shear gas bubbles or liquid droplets down to micron sizes.

quantitative_guidelines.tip_speeds: Blending: 5 to 10 ft/s (1.5 to 3 m/s); Reaction/Suspension: 10 to 15 ft/s (3 to 4.5 m/s); Dispersion: 15 to 22 ft/s (4.5 to 6.7 m/s).

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure shaft critical speed is at least 20% to 30% above operating speed to avoid resonance vibration.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich p. 578; Excel sheet 'Mixing'.

rules.rule: In cylindrical agitated vessels, standard geometry specifies: liquid height H_liq = 1.0 to 1.5 times vessel diameter; total vessel height H_tank = 1.5 to 2.0 times diameter. Install 4 vertical wall baffles with width W_b = D_vessel / 10 to D_vessel / 12 (typically 1/12 D) to suppress central surface vortexing and convert swirling flow into top-to-bottom circulation.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Without baffles, fluid swirls as a solid body with very little relative velocity between fluid layers, pulling a deep surface air vortex that can unseat the impeller. Wall baffles disrupt circumferential momentum, forcing flow down the shaft and up the vessel walls.

quantitative_guidelines.baffle_width: W_b = D_vessel / 12 (or D / 10 for low-viscosity fluids)
quantitative_guidelines.baffle_wall_clearance: Clearance from wall ~ 0.15 * W_b to prevent solids accumulation behind baffles.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: In viscous liquids (> 10-20 Pa s), baffles cause stagnant dead zones behind them; unbaffled vessels or off-center shafts are preferred.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich p. 579; Excel sheet 'Mixing'.

rules.rule: For gas sparging in corrosive or simple agitated vessels without mechanical impellers, specify gas rates per square meter of tank cross-section: 1. Mild agitation: 0.004 m3/(s m2) [0.8 cfm/ft2]. 2. Relatively complete agitation: 0.008 m3/(s m2) [1.6 cfm/ft2]. 3. Violent agitation: 0.02 m3/(s m2) [4.0 cfm/ft2].
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Rising gas bubbles pump surrounding liquid upward by buoyancy (airlift effect). While energy efficiency is lower than mechanical impellers, spargers avoid rotating shaft seals in highly toxic, corrosive, or high-pressure reactors.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Sparging alone provides poor solids suspension for particles > 100 microns with settling velocity > 0.01 m/s.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Ulrich & Vasudevan Appendix C (Mixers, p. 578).

materials_of_construction.name: Materials of Construction (MOC)
materials_of_construction.description: Rules for selecting carbon steel, austenitic stainless steels, nickel alloys, titanium, and corrosion allowances.

rules.rule: Carbon steel is the lowest cost and most common structural material for chemical plant equipment. It provides excellent resistance to dry gases, hydrocarbons, non-corrosive organic solvents, alkaline streams (pH > 8 to 14), and concentrated sulfuric acid (> 70 wt% at ambient temperatures). However, it has very poor resistance to dilute acids and strong chlorides, and exhibits brittle impact fracture below -29 C (-20 F) without Charpy V-notch impact testing.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Carbon steel forms a protective passivating carbonate or oxide film in alkaline or non-aqueous media. In dilute acids, hydrogen evolution rapidly dissolves iron. Low temperatures cause a transition from ductile shear failure to brittle cleavage fracture (ductile-to-brittle transition).

quantitative_guidelines.temperature_limit_low: -29 C (-20 F) standard; requires impact-tested fine-grain steel down to -46 C (-50 F)
quantitative_guidelines.temperature_limit_high: 425 C (800 F) max, above which graphitization and severe creep occur
quantitative_guidelines.standard_corrosion_allowance: 1.5 to 3.0 mm (1/16 to 1/8 inch) added to calculated pressure wall thickness.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Never use carbon steel for moist acidic streams or when product iron contamination / discoloration cannot be tolerated.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.4; Sinnott & Towler Section 1.5; Excel sheet 'MOC'.

rules.rule: Specify austenitic stainless steels (Type 304, 316, 316L) for nitric acid, organic acids, food, pharmaceutical, and high-purity applications. Type 316 (containing 2-3% Molybdenum) provides superior resistance to localized pitting and crevice corrosion. CRITICAL WARNING: Austenitic stainless steels suffer catastrophic stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in the presence of trace chloride ions at temperatures exceeding 60 C (140 F); use duplex stainless steels (e.g. 2205) or nickel alloys instead.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Stainless steel passivity depends on a microscopic, self-healing chromium oxide (Cr2O3) film. Chloride ions penetrate and break down this passive layer locally; combined with residual tensile stresses, transgranular micro-cracks propagate rapidly, causing sudden catastrophic brittle failure.

quantitative_guidelines.chloride_scc_threshold: > 60 C (140 F) with Cl- concentrations as low as 10 to 50 ppm
quantitative_guidelines.low_carbon_grade: Use 'L' grades (304L, 316L, C <= 0.03%) for welded construction to prevent intergranular sensitization / chromium carbide precipitation.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Do not insulate stainless steel with chloride-bearing insulation without waterproof barriers (ASTM C795).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.4; Sinnott & Towler Section 1.5; Excel sheet 'MOC'.

rules.rule: Specify specialized corrosion-resistant alloys for extreme chemical environments: 1. Monel (70Ni-30Cu): excellent for hydrofluoric acid (HF), seawater, and non-oxidizing salts. 2. Inconel (Ni-Cr-Fe): for high-temperature oxidation (> 800 C) and carburizing atmospheres. 3. Hastelloy (Ni-Mo-Cr, e.g. C-276): superior resistance to hot hydrochloric acid, wet chlorine, and mixed reducing/oxidizing acids. 4. Titanium: outstanding resistance to wet chlorine gas, chlorates, and seawater; DANGER: Titanium ignites and burns pyrophorically in dry chlorine gas (moisture content must exceed 1.5% to maintain passivity).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Nickel forms exceptionally stable passive complexes in aggressive acidic and alkaline regimes where iron-based lattices dissolve. Titanium develops a rock-hard titanium dioxide (TiO2) film that resists chlorides but requires trace water molecules to self-repair.

quantitative_guidelines.titanium_moisture_limit: Minimum 1.5 to 2.0 wt% H2O required in wet chlorine to prevent pyrophoric combustion
quantitative_guidelines.hastelloy_c276: Resists HCl at all concentrations up to 50 C, and boiling dilute HCl
quantitative_guidelines.monel_hf_acid: Industry standard for HF alkylation units.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: High raw material cost (Hastelloy is 10-15x more expensive than carbon steel); use clad plate or loose linings where feasible.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.4; Sinnott & Towler Section 1.5; Excel sheet 'MOC'.

rules.rule: Specify design corrosion allowances based on fluid corrosivity: 1. Non-corrosive hydrocarbons and refined chemicals: 1.5 mm (1/16 inch). 2. Mildly corrosive process fluids and boiler steam: 3.0 mm (1/8 inch). 3. Highly corrosive environments: if required corrosion allowance exceeds 6.0 mm (1/4 inch) over a 20-year design life, do not add steel thickness; upgrade metallurgy to a corrosion-resistant alloy, cladding, or polymer/glass lining.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Adding carbon steel thickness beyond 6 mm produces heavy, difficult-to-weld vessels without guaranteeing integrity against localized pitting or stress corrosion. Clad plate (e.g. 3 mm 316L explosion-bonded to 25 mm carbon steel) provides both structural strength and corrosion resistance at reasonable cost.

quantitative_guidelines.cladding_thickness: Typically 2.5 to 3.5 mm alloy on carbon steel backing.

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Heat exchanger tubes are thin-walled (1.2 to 2.1 mm / 18 to 14 BWG); no corrosion allowance is possible; tubes must be made of corrosion-resistant material.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Sinnott & Towler Section 1.5; Turton Table 11.4; Excel sheet 'MOC'.

physical_properties_and_shortcuts.name: Physical Properties & Shortcut Approximations
physical_properties_and_shortcuts.description: Rules of thumb and benchmark values for liquid/gas densities, heat capacities, latent heats, Trouton's rule, and viscosities.

rules.rule: For order-of-magnitude preliminary design and verification: 1. Water density: ~1,000 kg/m3 (62.4 lb/ft3 / 8.33 lb/gal). 2. Typical organic liquids / hydrocarbons: 700 to 900 kg/m3 (44 to 56 lb/ft3 / SG = 0.70 to 0.90). 3. Chlorinated solvents: 1,200 to 1,500 kg/m3 (75 to 94 lb/ft3 / SG = 1.2 to 1.5). 4. Atmospheric air / ideal gas at 20 C: 1.2 kg/m3 (0.075 lb/ft3). Gas density scales with ideal gas law: rho_gas = (P * MW) / (R * T).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Liquid hydrocarbons have lower density than water due to open tetrahedral carbon chains; halogenated hydrocarbons are denser due to heavy halogen atomic weights.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Near the thermodynamic critical point (T_r > 0.9), liquid density drops sharply and compressibility expands.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.2(a); Excel sheet 'Physical Properties'.

rules.rule: Use shortcut heat capacities (C_p) for rapid thermal checks: 1. Liquid water: 4.18 kJ/(kg K) [1.0 Btu/(lb F)]. 2. Typical organic liquids: 1.5 to 2.5 kJ/(kg K) [0.35 to 0.60 Btu/(lb F)] (roughly half that of water). 3. Steam: ~2.0 kJ/(kg K) [0.48 Btu/(lb F)]. 4. Air and diatomic gases: ~1.0 kJ/(kg K) [0.24 Btu/(lb F)]. 5. Solid minerals / metals: 0.4 to 0.9 kJ/(kg K) [0.10 to 0.22 Btu/(lb F)].
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Water has an exceptionally high heat capacity due to extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding networks. Organic liquids lack this cohesive hydrogen-bonding lattice and therefore require only ~40-60% of the thermal energy per kilogram to achieve the same temperature rise.
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Heat capacities rise significantly with temperature; use polynomial temperature correlations for accurate high-temperature exchanger design.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.2(a); Excel sheet 'Physical Properties'.

rules.rule: Estimate latent heat of vaporization (lambda): 1. Water at 1 atm: ~2,260 kJ/kg (970 Btu/lb). 2. Typical organic solvents and hydrocarbons: 250 to 400 kJ/kg (110 to 175 Btu/lb) (roughly 1/6 to 1/8 that of water). 3. Estimate molar heat of vaporization for non-polar liquids using Trouton's Rule: Delta H_vap / T_b ~ 88 J/(mol K) [21 cal/(mol K)], where T_b is normal boiling point in Kelvin.
rules.explanation_and_derivation: Trouton's rule reflects the nearly constant entropy change of vaporization (Delta S_vap ~ 88 J/(mol K)) when an unordered liquid expands into an ideal gas. Highly hydrogen-bonded fluids (water, alcohols, carboxylic acids) have higher Delta S_vap (~105-115 J/(mol K)).
rules.conditions_and_limitations: Latent heat decreases with temperature, vanishing to zero at the thermodynamic critical temperature (Watson correlation: Delta H_2 = Delta H_1 * ((1 - T_r2)/(1 - T_r1))^0.38).
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.2(a); Excel sheet 'Physical Properties'.

rules.rule: Shortcut viscosity benchmarks: 1. Water at 20 C: 1.0 cP (1.0 mPa s = 0.001 Pa s = 0.000672 lb/(ft s)). 2. Light liquid hydrocarbons: 0.2 to 0.8 cP. 3. Viscous organics / light oils: 2.0 to 10 cP. 4. Heavy fuel oils / polymers: 50 to 1,000+ cP. 5. Common gases at atmospheric pressure: 0.01 to 0.02 cP (10 to 20 micro-Pa s). Liquid viscosity decreases exponentially with temperature (Andrade equation); gas viscosity increases with temperature (mu_gas ~ T^0.7).
rules.explanation_and_derivation: In liquids, momentum transfer occurs across intermolecular potential wells that are disrupted by thermal kinetic motion (viscosity drops with T). In gases, viscosity arises from molecular collisions, whose frequency and momentum transfer increase with molecular thermal velocity (viscosity rises with T).

quantitative_guidelines.water_viscosity: 1.00 cP at 20 C; 0.28 cP at 100 C
quantitative_guidelines.centipoise_conversion: 1 cP = 1 mPa s = 0.001 Pa s = 2.42 lb/(ft hr)

rules.conditions_and_limitations: Ensure fluid shear behavior is Newtonian before applying standard Reynolds number equations; non-Newtonian slurries require rheometry.
rules.variations_and_discrepancies: Turton Table 11.2(a) & 11.2(b); Excel sheet 'Physical Properties'.
